title: Jays tickets, drums and Tinder: Hundreds of purchases made with Toronto city credit cards raise questions about misuse
summary: City of Toronto employees used city credit cards to make hundreds of purchases that included Blue Jays tickets, gift cards and later-disputed purchases on Tinder, an analysis of expenditure data by…

image.caption: An analysis of City of Toronto credit card expenditure data by CBC News has found that city staff spent thousands of dollars on purchases that appear questionable. (Yulia Grigoryeva/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: City of Toronto employees used city credit cards to make hundreds of purchases that included Blue Jays tickets, gift cards and later-disputed purchases on Tinder, an analysis of expenditure data by CBC News has found.

The transactions are documented in a list of expense records made publicly available by the City of Toronto. They detail the spending habits of 88 city divisions through their use of city-issued credit cards, also known as purchasing cards or PCards.

While meant to ease bottlenecks for low-dollar purchases like office supplies, a snapshot of recorded expenses analyzed by CBC News found some transactions appeared questionable, with several legal, financial and policy experts saying the PCard program requires better oversight.
CBC News shared its findings with the city and Mayor Olivia Chow's office, alongside a list of extensive questions about the PCard program.
Chow's office did not acknowledge the request for comment or respond to an interview request. The city did not respond to an interview request.

blocks.text: Mark Rozic, the city's director of accounting services, said in a statement that while PCard transaction data is publicly available, it "does not tell the full story of what was purchased, why it was needed, or the city service or activity it supported."
CBC News did ask the city to provide supporting documentation to help explain transactions that appeared questionable, which the city did not provide.
Instead, Rozic said the PCard program has "multiple layers of oversight" that include spending limits and restrictions, mandatory training and management review.

"The City takes its stewardship of public funds seriously and expects all cardholders and approvers to use City purchasing cards responsibly, transparently and in accordance with program requirements,” he said.
The findings come as the city grapples with its financial outlook and looks to find additional revenue tools to support its books.

CBC News also reached out to CUPE 79 for comment, a local union branch whose members include City of Toronto workers. Spokesperson Tor Sandberg said in a statement Thursday that the union can't provide comment because it's unclear whether the PCard purchases in question were made by management or the front-line staff it represents.
How Toronto's new revenue ideas could hit your wallet
How we tracked this information and what we found

The city's PCard data has over 800,000 entries, with expenditures for several city divisions going back over a decade. Not every division had updated transaction records or records that went back that far.

CBC News picked eight city divisions and conducted a line-by-line review of their transactions. Transactions that appeared questionable were then put into a spreadsheet that was shared with experts, Toronto's auditor general, the city and the mayor's office.
The spreadsheet included purchases from the following city divisions:

items: Seniors and long-term care: $1,986 for Blue Jays tickets bought in 2026.
Toronto Water: $169.50 spent on "other expenses" at Coach in 2023.
Toronto paramedics: $1,283.34 for drums bought at Long and McQuade in 2025.
City clerks: $146.89 for a "world deluxe subscription" with Ancestry.ca in 2025.
Environment: $100 for a "presentation of appreciation item" bought at Body Blitz, a downtown spa, in 2023.

blocks.text: "On the surface … this is weird," said Zac Spicer, an associate professor at York University's school of public policy, who reviewed a snapshot of the recorded expenses for CBC News.

"This is public money there. The [city] should be willing to sort of justify what is happening here," he said, noting that while PCards are meant to ease administrative burdens, they don't mean "unchecked spending."

Among the expenses analyzed by CBC News, thousands do appear to check out: $196.56 paid by Toronto 311 for an order of office binders, $451.32 worth of soccer balls bought by the FIFA secretariat for the city's Soccer For All mini pitches, $85.03 for screws, ceiling tiles and plywood bought by Toronto Water.
Some also appear to be disputed, including a total of $249.95 spent on Tinder by Toronto Water in 2016.
Thousands of PCard expenditures do appear to check out, such as purchases made for building supplies by Toronto Water and soccer balls by Toronto's FIFA secretariat. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)
City did not provide PCard policy
CBC News asked the City of Toronto for a document that outlined its PCard spending policies. The city did not provide one. No public document outlining how the city uses the cards was found.

In an emailed statement, Frédérique Mazerolle, spokesperson for the city, said the program provides city divisions with a "convenient and cost-effective way to make certain purchases on behalf of the city."

Mazerolle said each PCard has set transaction and monthly spending limits as well as restrictions on the types of purchases that can be made. Only certain city staff get authorization to use the cards, she said.

Eligible PCard expenses are those needed for city business and permitted by its purchasing rules, such as certain office supplies, subscriptions, pre-authorized business travel and emergency purchases, Mazerolle said.
Many divisions recorded all-time spending highs
Paul Emanuelli, a procurement lawyer in Toronto with knowledge of the PCard system, said some of the expenditures identified by CBC News reflect inadequate record-keeping by the city.
"Many of these expenditures, they're really hard, on the surface, to really explain what they're for," he said.
Paul Emanuelli, a Toronto procurement lawyer, says some of the PCard transactions identified by CBC News reflect inadequate record-keeping by the city. (Paul Borkwood/CBC)
Several city divisions had their annual PCard spending reach over $1 million. Divisions with some of the highest PCard expenditures for a single recorded year included:

items: Parks and recreation: $10 million spent in 2025.
Seniors and long-term care: $1.89 million spent in 2026.
Shelter and support: $1.36 million spent in 2025.

blocks.text: If the transactions are publicly listed online, they should be able to stand on their own and be "self-evident," Emanuelli said.
"In procurement, one of the foundational concepts is transparency, because it's public expenditure. A fragmented disclosure is not useful."

Auditor general should review: forensic accountant
CBC News identified 44 of the 88 city divisions had PCard spending reach an all-time high this year, or for their latest reported full year.
Some divisions, like environment, have had spending reach an all-time high in 2026, despite the year not being over yet.
Some divisions are also using the cards more than ever, with the number of transactions increasing for 40 out of the 88 divisions in 2026 or their latest reported full year, according to the data.

Charles Smedmor, a forensic accountant who's previously worked with former Toronto Auditor General Jeff Griffiths, said the expenses identified by CBC News warrant a closer review by city council or the current auditor general, Tara Anderson.
"Looking at it, some [expenses] are red flags, some are orange flags, some are reasonable," he said.
"These sorts of things have to be followed up."
Smedmor said the city should provide supporting documents related to each expense in order to get a clearer sense of what transactions can be deemed reasonable.

blocks.text: City auditor general recommended increasing PCard use

From a procurement standpoint, Emanuelli said he was "pleasantly surprised" to see many of the city's PCard expenditures appeared well documented and justifiable. But the expenses that appeared inappropriate are still a "serious matter," especially if the PCard program continues to expand, something the city's auditor general recommended last year.

It's not the first time this recommendation has been made. In 2009, the auditor general also recommended the city expand its PCard program, with the caveat that it also improve PCard training, overall policy, and safeguards.
City council adopted the recommendation in 2010, but Anderson's 2025 audit notes it has "remained open for more than 15 years."
Toronto pauses most hiring due to financial pressures
The audit's executive summary said staff and management voiced concerns PCard rules limited "operational efficiency," and they recommended their use be increased, according to the audit.

At the same time, the audit acknowledged there was minimal data available to figure out where bottlenecks were happening. It recommended the city consider expanding PCard use anyway, so long as additional resources were provided on how to appropriately use the cards, such as refresher training each year.

blocks.text: Alexandra Galanis, spokesperson for the auditor general, said the office cannot comment on the expenditure data shared by CBC News because it would need to review additional "contextual information and supporting documents" from city divisions.
She said every city division is responsible for "line-by-line" reviews of PCard expenditures, and authorizing managers "must ensure proper oversight of PCard use within their division."
"Our office takes matters related to misuse of funds seriously," Galanis said in an emailed statement.
Galanis also acknowledged the recommendation to expand PCard use has been open for over a decade, but it's the only recommendation — out of 20 made in 2009 — that remains open.
